Need to search first.I couldn't get through all three parts of the research. The search tool hit its usage limit partway through, and the full-page reader stopped working after one page. So these notes come from one full Enduring Word page and the page extracts that searches returned. Most points come from Bible Hub and StudyLight pages that collect several older commentaries on one verse; I've named the commentator only where the extract made it clear.

**What's missing:**
- **Part 2 (Protestant disagreements):** I found nothing from a tradition's own teachers saying how they differ on these verses. The obvious candidates are how vv. 2–3 (the Sabbath) apply to Christians and what the "filling with the Spirit" in v. 31 means. My Ligonier searches failed, so I've included no claims about differences between traditions.
- **Part 3 (other views):** I reached none of the scholarly (NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey), Catholic, Orthodox or prosperity-teaching sources, so that part is left out.
- **Verses with no notes:** I found nothing specific on vv. 6–9 or 10–19 beyond the general remarks under those verses.

---

**vv. 1–3: The Sabbath comes first**
- Before the building work begins, Israel is reminded to enter God's rest. Guzik applies this to Christians: work for God should grow out of resting in Him and His finished work. He also says plain obedience has to come before working for the Lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/
- George Bush (quoted at Precept Austin) says not even the tabernacle work could be done on the Sabbath. He takes this to mean the holy day ranked above the holy place. He reads the phrase "sabbath of sabbatism" as a picture of the eternal rest still waiting for God's people. A note on the same page points out the pattern of Exodus 31–35: the Sabbath reminder comes just before the passage about craftsmen filled with the Spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-35-commentary

**v. 2: "Must be put to death"**
- GotQuestions says the penalty shows how serious the Sabbath was as the sign of God's covenant with Israel. Israel's excitement about building must not crowd out worship. In Christian terms, the death penalty pictures the fate of those who will not rest in Christ's finished work (Hebrews 4; 10). https://www.gotquestions.org/working-on-the-Sabbath.html
- Precept Austin admits the penalty sounds severe. It says the aim was to teach holiness and trust that God would provide on a day without work, and it links this verse to the man stoned for gathering wood (Numbers 15:32–36). https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-35-commentary
- A Bible Hub article draws three points:
  - Like other covenant signs, the Sabbath carried life-and-death consequences.
  - The penalty protected servants from bosses who would overwork them.
  - Colossians 2:16–17 calls the Sabbath a shadow whose substance is Christ.
  https://biblehub.com/q/Why_death_for_Sabbath_work_in_Exodus.htm

**v. 3: No fire**
- **Gill:** probably a temporary rule tied to building the tabernacle. It stopped people heating tools or melting metal on the Sabbath. It wasn't a total ban, since mercy and necessity (cold, sick people, babies) would require fire. He describes strict Jewish practice and the rabbis' exception for the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-3.htm
- **Another older commentator on the same page:** the ban targets fire for the tabernacle work, not cooking. He notes Jesus went to a Sabbath meal (Luke 14) and that this rule is not called "perpetual." Another note on the page (quoting a "Mr. Scott") observes that Scripture never mentions anyone being punished for kindling a fire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-3.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** making fire took real labour (rubbing sticks together), and in a warm climate it was mostly for cooking, already forbidden in Exodus 16:23. Karaite Jews keep the rule literally, while most Jews saw it as temporary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-3.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** the rule had to be kept even for the tabernacle work. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-3.htm
- **Clarke (quoted by Guzik):** Jews took the rule to ban fire for work or cooking, but allowed it for light and heat. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/

**v. 4: "This is what the LORD has commanded"**
- This begins carrying out what God told Moses in Exodus 25–31. Cole (quoted by Guzik) says the repetition is deliberate, to show Moses was faithful. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/

**v. 5: A willing heart**
- **Guzik:** God could have provided the materials by miracle. Instead He funds His work through His people's willing gifts, because they need to be a giving people. He links this to 2 Corinthians 9:7 ("God loves a cheerful giver"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/
- **Precept Austin:** "heart" here means the will, and God doesn't want manipulated giving. Bush notes that the Hebrew word for "willing" (*nadib*) can also mean noble or generous, and that Moses set no amounts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-35-commentary

**vv. 6–9: The materials**
- Guzik simply notes these are the materials listed in Exodus 25–31. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/

**vv. 10–19: The craftsmen and the work**
- The labour was to come from Israel's own skilled craftsmen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/

**v. 20: The people go home**
- Guzik: Moses sent the people home to decide what to give. There was no quick public pledge and no contest between tribes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/

**v. 21: Hearts stirred**
- Bush: literally "whose heart lifted him up," meaning a heart raised to cheerful readiness. Precept Austin adds that the people did the right thing for the right reason, because God wants our hearts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-35-commentary
- Guzik: the gifts were plainly given to the LORD, not to Moses or the nation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/

**v. 22: The gold jewellery**
- **Poole and Gill:** some of this jewellery had been kept back from the golden calf, perhaps especially by the women. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-22.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** remembering the calf may have made the people keener to give now, as a sign of repentance. Giving up their ornaments put beautifying God's house ahead of their own appearance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/35-22.html
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** the Hebrew suggests the women gave first. There were no coins then, and jewellery served as money.
- **Ellicott:** the exact items are uncertain; the last word probably means a bead necklace.
- **Barnes:** private luxury was given up for God's honour.
  (All three at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-22.htm)
- **Calvin:** giving up rings, which many won't part with even when starving, showed real zeal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/35-22.html
- **Wave offering:** Keil & Delitzsch explain that the word means to swing to and fro, a gesture used to dedicate gifts to the Lord. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-3.htm

**vv. 23–24: Other gifts**
- Matthew Henry: people gave what they had. Those without jewels brought goats' hair and ram skins, and God looks more at the giver's heart than at the gift's value. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/35-26.html

**vv. 25–26: The women's work**
- **Matthew Henry:** some women spun fine coloured yarn and others plain goats' hair, yet both are called "wise." God accepts humble work as well as fine work, and humble work done for God's honour will be rewarded. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/35-26.html
- **Matthew Henry (Concise):** people faithful in lowly jobs are as accepted by God as those in splendid ones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-26.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary and Gill (citing Aben Ezra):** spinning goats' hair took special skill. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-26.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** the yarn was dyed before weaving, as in Egypt, and spinning was traditionally women's work (Proverbs 31:19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-26.htm
- Guzik and Cole: everyone, from rulers to women spinning goats' hair, had a part (Ephesians 4:16). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/

**vv. 27–28: The leaders' gifts**
- **Ellicott:** probably the twelve tribal princes, each giving the breastpiece stone that bore his tribe's name.
- **Barnes:** the rulers were wealthier than others.
- **Gill:** they are listed last perhaps because they brought what others didn't have. He mentions a Jewish view that a letter missing from the Hebrew word "rulers" hints they were slow to give.
- **Pulpit Commentary:** these were the "princes" Moses appointed on Jethro's advice (Exodus 18:25).
  (All at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-27.htm)

**v. 29: A freewill offering**
- Guzik: the repeated stress on freedom and no pressure. Willing hearts still need clear direction on what, when and how to give. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/

**v. 30: "Called by name"**
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** now that the materials were collected, Moses fittingly reminded the people that God Himself had appointed the men who would handle their gold. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-31.htm
- **Bush:** Bezalel's name means "under the shadow of God," though Bush sees no special significance in it here. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary

**v. 31: Filled with the Spirit of God**
- **Calvin:** "filled with the Spirit" shows these gifts were neither natural nor earned. All talents come from the Spirit, but special gifts like these do so in a higher way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/35-31.html
- **Matthew Henry:** skill even in ordinary trades is God's gift (James 1:17) and should be used for His honour. He compares the apostles, "master-builders" filled with the Spirit for the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/35-31.html
- **Guzik:** a special outpouring of the Holy Spirit, needed because the work had to follow God's exact pattern (Exodus 25:9). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-35/
- **Precept Austin (Exodus 31 notes):** these men held no priestly or prophetic office, yet still needed the Spirit for their craft. Bush sees this as gifts of mind close to divine inspiration, with no claim about their moral character. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-31-commentary

**vv. 32–33: The crafts**
- Pulpit Commentary and Gill note these verses repeat Exodus 31:3–5 almost word for word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-31.htm

**v. 34: The ability to teach**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** God equipped Bezalel and Oholiab to train and supervise workers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-31.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** those who lead should teach, and the knowledgeable should share their skill rather than keep it to themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/35-31.html
- **Matthew Henry (Concise):** he criticises those who tell others what to do but won't lift a finger themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-31.htm

**v. 35: Every kind of craft**
- Keil & Delitzsch read the closing words as "doers of every work and inventors of designs." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/35-31.htm
